discovery: Proposal of electron- and nuclear-spin qubits in semiconductors (quantum dots and donors in silicon), founding solid-state spin quantum computing

nominees.name: David P. DiVincenzo
nominees.affiliation: RWTH Aachen University and Forschungszentrum Jülich, Germany

nominees.name: Bruce E. Kane
nominees.affiliation: Laboratory for Physical Sciences, University of Maryland, USA

motivation: In 1998 Loss and DiVincenzo showed that the spin of a single electron confined in a semiconductor quantum dot could act as a qubit, with gates driven by electrically controlled exchange. In the same year Kane proposed encoding quantum information in the nuclear and electron spins of phosphorus donors in isotopically purified silicon, addressed by surface gates. These were bold, long-horizon proposals. They turned the semiconductor physics behind modern electronics into a blueprint for quantum hardware. Over twenty-five years, laboratories worldwide have realised them: single-shot spin readout, coherence times of seconds, one- and two-qubit gates above fault-tolerance thresholds, and multi-qubit processors made in industrial CMOS foundries. DiVincenzo's criteria also became the universal checklist for any quantum computer. Spin qubits in silicon are now a leading route to scalable, manufacturable quantum computation. This work is fundamental, has been confirmed many times over, and is changing technology.
